subject: Renal
vignette: A 3-year-old child is brought in by a parent who noticed a large, painless unilateral flank mass. Urinalysis shows hematuria, and the blood pressure is elevated. Imaging demonstrates a large solid renal mass, and histology reveals embryonic glomerular structures.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is the most common renal malignancy of early childhood, typically ages 2-4. It contains embryonic glomerular structures and presents with a large, palpable, unilateral flank mass and/or hematuria with possible hypertension.

explanation_incorrect.A: Neuroblastoma is a common pediatric extracranial solid tumor but arises from the adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain, is usually suprarenal, and does not contain embryonic glomeruli.
explanation_incorrect.C: Renal cell carcinoma is predominantly an adult tumor and is not the classic cause of a large flank mass in a 2-to-4-year-old child.
explanation_incorrect.D: Mesoblastic nephroma is a usually benign congenital renal tumor that presents in infancy, often in the first year of life, rather than at age 2-4.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hydronephrosis is dilation of the collecting system from obstruction, not a solid mass containing embryonic glomerular structures.

educationalObjective: Wilms tumor is the most common renal malignancy of early childhood and presents with a large unilateral flank mass, hematuria, and possible hypertension.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 4-year-old with Wilms tumor also has aniridia (absence of the iris), genitourinary malformations, and a range of developmental delays. Genetic testing demonstrates a deletion involving a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11.
question: Which syndrome is most consistent with these findings, and which genetic lesion causes it?
explanation_correct: WAGR complex consists of Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary malformations, and a Range of developmental delays, and it results from a WT1 deletion on chromosome 11. The chromosome 11 location is recalled by the mnemonic W11ms tumor.

explanation_incorrect.A: Denys-Drash syndrome results from a WT1 point mutation and features diffuse mesangial sclerosis and gonadal dysgenesis, not aniridia or developmental delay.
explanation_incorrect.B: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is an imprinting defect at WT2 with organomegaly, macroglossia, hemihyperplasia, and omphalocele, not aniridia or genitourinary malformations.
explanation_incorrect.C: WAGR complex is caused by a WT1 deletion, not a WT2 deletion; WT2 alterations are associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Denys-Drash syndrome is due to a WT1 point mutation and does not include aniridia or developmental delay; both the syndrome and the gene pairing are incorrect.

educationalObjective: WAGR complex (Wilms, aniridia, GU malformations, developmental delay) is caused by a WT1 deletion on chromosome 11.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 3-year-old boy with Wilms tumor develops early-onset nephrotic syndrome. Renal biopsy shows diffuse mesangial sclerosis, and he has male pseudohermaphroditism from gonadal dysgenesis. A germline mutation in a chromosome 11 tumor suppressor gene is identified.
question: Which of the following syndromes best fits this presentation?
explanation_correct: Denys-Drash syndrome consists of Wilms tumor, Diffuse mesangial sclerosis causing early-onset nephrotic syndrome, and Dysgenesis of gonads (male pseudohermaphroditism), due to a WT1 mutation. The three D's are the classic board association.

explanation_incorrect.A: WAGR complex includes Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary malformations, and developmental delay from a WT1 deletion; it does not feature diffuse mesangial sclerosis or gonadal dysgenesis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome features organomegaly, macroglossia, hemihyperplasia, and omphalocele from a WT2 imprinting defect, not mesangial sclerosis or pseudohermaphroditism.
explanation_incorrect.D: Potter sequence results from oligohydramnios due to bilateral renal agenesis with characteristic facies and limb anomalies, not from a Wilms tumor.
explanation_incorrect.E: Alport syndrome is a hereditary nephritis with hematuria, sensorineural hearing loss, and lens abnormalities from type IV collagen deficiency; it is not associated with Wilms tumor or gonadal dysgenesis.

educationalObjective: Denys-Drash syndrome pairs Wilms tumor with diffuse mesangial sclerosis and gonadal dysgenesis via a WT1 mutation.

subject: Renal
vignette: An infant is noted at birth to have macroglossia, hemihyperplasia, and an omphalocele, with marked organomegaly on examination. The child is at increased risk of developing Wilms tumor. The underlying mechanism is an imprinting defect that causes overexpression of a growth-promoting gene on chromosome 11.
question: Which of the following best identifies the syndrome and its genetic mechanism?

options.text: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome due to an imprinting defect causing WT2 overexpression
WAGR complex due to a WT1 deletion
Denys-Drash syndrome due to a WT1 point mutation
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome due to a WT1 deletion
WAGR complex due to an imprinting defect at WT2

explanation_correct: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome features organomegaly, macroglossia, hemihyperplasia, and omphalocele. It is caused by an imprinting defect leading to genetic overexpression of growth-promoting genes including WT2 on chromosome 11, and it predisposes to Wilms tumor.

explanation_incorrect.B: WAGR complex is due to a WT1 deletion and produces aniridia, genitourinary malformations, and developmental delay rather than macroglossia and omphalocele.
explanation_incorrect.C: Denys-Drash syndrome is a WT1 point mutation with diffuse mesangial sclerosis and gonadal dysgenesis, not hemihyperplasia or organomegaly.
explanation_incorrect.D: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is linked to WT2 and an imprinting defect, not to a WT1 deletion.
explanation_incorrect.E: WAGR complex is caused by a WT1 deletion rather than a WT2 imprinting defect; the syndrome and mechanism are mismatched.

educationalObjective: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (organomegaly, macroglossia, hemihyperplasia, omphalocele) arises from imprinting defect with WT2 overexpression and raises Wilms tumor risk.

subject: Renal
vignette: A genetics lecture reviews the molecular basis of Wilms tumor. The speaker emphasizes that loss-of-function mutations of specific tumor suppressor genes are implicated and uses the mnemonic W11ms tumor to help recall the chromosomal location of these genes.
question: Which genes and chromosome are correctly paired in this mnemonic?
explanation_correct: Wilms tumor can be associated with loss-of-function mutations of the tumor suppressor genes WT1 or WT2, both located on chromosome 11 (W11ms tumor). WT1 deletion causes WAGR, WT1 mutation causes Denys-Drash, and a WT2 imprinting defect causes Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: Chromosome 17 is not the location of WT1 or WT2; the W11ms mnemonic points specifically to chromosome 11.
explanation_incorrect.B: Chromosome 7 does not harbor WT1 or WT2; the Wilms tumor suppressor genes are on chromosome 11.
explanation_incorrect.C: The classic genes are WT1 and WT2; WT3 is not part of the described set of Wilms tumor suppressor genes.
explanation_incorrect.E: Chromosome 22 is associated with tumors such as neurofibromatosis type 2, not Wilms tumor; WT1 and WT2 reside on chromosome 11.

educationalObjective: Wilms tumor is linked to loss-of-function mutations in WT1 or WT2 on chromosome 11.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 2-year-old girl has a large unilateral abdominal mass. The resected mass shows immature renal tissue containing embryonic glomerular structures, consistent with a tumor derived from metanephric blastema.
question: Which of the following histologic findings is characteristic of this tumor?
explanation_correct: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is a pediatric renal malignancy composed of embryonic glomerular structures, reflecting its origin from immature metanephric tissue. It presents as a large unilateral flank mass, sometimes with hematuria and hypertension.

explanation_incorrect.A: Psammoma bodies are laminated calcifications seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous ovarian tumors, and papillary renal cell carcinoma, not in Wilms tumor.
explanation_incorrect.C: Signet-ring cells are typical of mucinous adenocarcinomas such as gastric cancer, not of this embryonic renal tumor.
explanation_incorrect.D: Clear cells with abundant glycogen are characteristic of clear cell renal cell carcinoma, an adult tumor, not Wilms tumor.
explanation_incorrect.E: Squamous metaplasia is associated with chronic irritation such as in bladder squamous cell carcinoma, not with Wilms tumor.

educationalObjective: The presence of embryonic glomerular structures in a pediatric renal mass identifies Wilms tumor.
